n: At dawn the council meets formally to confirm the death sentence, since night trials were considered improper.
Under Roman rule the Jewish council couldn’t carry out executions, so they bind Jesus and hand him over to Pilate, the Roman governor.

f.g: Roman governor (prefect) of Judea about AD 26–36; an inscription bearing his name was found at Caesarea in 1961.

n: Seeing Jesus condemned, Judas is overcome with remorse and tries to return the thirty silver coins.

f.g: Greek metamelomai — felt regret or remorse, a different word from the usual one for repentance.

n: Judas admits he has betrayed innocent blood. The leaders coldly reply, “That’s your problem.”

f.g: That’s your concern, not ours.

n: He throws the money into the temple and goes off and hangs himself — a tragic end of despair.
The chief priests, who paid the blood money, now scruple over putting it in the temple treasury — a striking picture of the hypocrisy Jesus condemned.

f.g: Greek korbanas — the temple treasury.

n: They use it to buy a potter’s field as a cemetery for foreigners who died in Jerusalem.

f.g: Perhaps a field where potters dug clay, no longer useful for farming.
Foreigners, visitors to Jerusalem.

n: The place became known as the Field of Blood.

f.g: Aramaic Akeldama.

n: Matthew sees prophecy fulfilled. The wording is mostly from Zechariah, combined with themes from Jeremiah about a potter and a purchased field.

f.g: Jeremy = Jeremiah.

n: The silver paid for the potter’s field, as the Lord had directed — the price at which Israel valued its Shepherd.
Pilate asks if Jesus is the King of the Jews — a political charge Rome would take seriously. Jesus answers, “You say so.”

f.w: Art thou the King of the Jews?

f.g: A guarded yes — true, but not in the sense you mean.

n: To the many accusations from the priests and elders, Jesus makes no reply.
Pilate presses him: doesn’t he hear all these charges?

f.w: how many things they witness against thee

n: Jesus doesn’t answer even one charge, and Pilate is amazed. Defendants normally fought for their lives.
It was the governor’s custom to release one prisoner chosen by the crowd at Passover.

f.g: was wont = was accustomed, usually did.

n: A notorious prisoner named Barabbas was being held — Mark and Luke say for rebellion and murder.

f.g: Aramaic “son of the father” — an ironic contrast with Jesus, the true Son of the Father.
Notorious, well known.

n: Pilate offers a choice: Barabbas or Jesus, “called Christ.”

f.w: Whom will ye that I release unto you?

n: Pilate realizes the leaders handed Jesus over out of envy, not justice.
While Pilate sits in judgment, his wife sends an urgent warning: have nothing to do with this righteous man; she has suffered in a dream about him.

f.g: Greek bēma — the official platform where a magistrate gave verdicts.

n: The leaders persuade the crowd to demand Barabbas and Jesus’s death.
Asked again which one to release, they shout, “Barabbas!”

f.g: Which of the two.

n: “Then what should I do with Jesus?” They all cry, “Crucify him!”
Pilate asks what crime he has committed; they only shout louder.
Fearing a riot, Pilate washes his hands publicly and declares himself innocent. But washing his hands cannot erase his responsibility.

f.g: A symbolic act of disclaiming guilt, also known in Jewish law.
A riot, uproar.

n: The crowd cries that the blood be on them and their children. Tragically, this verse was later misused to blame all Jews — a reading scripture and the Church reject; each person answers for his own sins.

f.w: His blood be on us, and on our children

n: Pilate frees Barabbas, has Jesus flogged, and hands him over to be crucified. Roman scourging with metal- or bone-tipped whips was brutal and sometimes fatal.

f.g: Whipped with a flagrum, a whip of leather straps weighted with bits of metal or bone.

n: The soldiers take Jesus into the governor’s headquarters and gather the whole cohort.

f.g: The praetorium — the governor’s official residence.
A cohort, up to 600 soldiers.

n: They strip him and throw a red military cloak over him, mocking him as a king in royal colors.

f.g: Probably a soldier’s red cloak, imitating royal purple.

n: They twist thorns into a crown, put a reed in his hand as a scepter, and kneel in mock homage: “Hail, King of the Jews!”

f.g: plaited = woven, braided.
Thorns are a symbol of the curse of the Fall; Christ wears them as he overcomes it.

n: They spit on him and beat him on the head with the reed.
Done mocking, they put his own clothes back on him and lead him out to be crucified.

f.w: led him away to crucify him

n: Weakened by the beating, Jesus can’t carry the cross beam. Soldiers force Simon of Cyrene, a passerby, to carry it.

f.g: A city in North Africa (modern Libya) with a large Jewish community.
Roman soldiers could legally force civilians into service.

n: They reach Golgotha, “the place of a skull,” just outside Jerusalem’s walls.

f.g: Aramaic for “skull”; Latin Calvaria gives us “Calvary.”

n: They offer him wine mixed with something bitter, probably a painkiller. He tastes it but refuses, choosing to face his suffering fully conscious.

f.g: Sour wine.
A bitter substance; Mark says myrrh.

n: They crucify him and gamble for his clothing — fulfilling Psalm 22.

f.g: Clothing; John says a seamless inner tunic.

n: The soldiers sit down to guard him until he dies.

f.g: Guarded him, to prevent any rescue.

n: Above his head is posted the charge: “This is Jesus the King of the Jews.” Meant as mockery, it is true.

f.w: THIS IS JESUS THE KING OF THE JEWS
f.g: John says it was written in Hebrew, Latin, and Greek.

n: Two criminals are crucified with him, one on each side — he is “numbered with the transgressors.”

f.g: Probably bandits or rebels (Greek lēstai).

f.w: one on the right hand, and another on the left

n: People passing by on the road hurl insults and shake their heads in scorn.

f.g: Insulted, abused.

n: They twist his words about the temple and taunt him to save himself — echoing Satan’s “If thou be the Son of God” in the wilderness.

f.w: If thou be the Son of God

n: The chief priests, scribes, and elders join in the mockery.
“He saved others; he can’t save himself.” Deep irony: it is precisely by not saving himself that he saves others.

f.w: He saved others; himself he cannot save

n: They taunt him with words from Psalm 22, unknowingly fulfilling the very psalm that describes his suffering.

f.w: He trusted in God; let him deliver him now

n: Even the two crucified with him join the insults. Luke records that one later repented.

f.w: cast the same in his teeth
f.g: Taunted him in the same way.

n: From noon until 3 p.m. darkness covers the land. In the Americas, the Book of Mormon records three days of darkness at his death.

f.g: About noon; the ninth hour is about 3 p.m.

n: Jesus cries out the opening words of Psalm 22 in Aramaic. Latter-day Saint leaders have taught that the Father withdrew his sustaining presence so the Son could finish the Atonement alone.

f.g: Abandoned, left alone.

n: Some bystanders mishear “Eli” as a call for Elijah, whom many believed would come to help the righteous in distress.

f.g: Elias = Elijah.

n: Someone runs to give him sour wine on a sponge lifted on a reed.

f.g: Cheap sour wine, the common drink of soldiers.

n: Others say, “Wait — let’s see if Elijah comes to rescue him.”

f.g: Leave him alone, wait.

n: Jesus cries out again with a loud voice and gives up his spirit. He doesn’t simply die — he voluntarily yields his life.

f.g: ghost = spirit. He released his spirit.

n: The temple veil, which separated the Holy of Holies from the rest of the temple, tears from top to bottom — as if by God’s hand. Through Christ the way into God’s presence is opened.

f.g: A heavy curtain before the Holy of Holies, where only the high priest entered once a year.

n: Tombs open, and many righteous people who had died are raised.

f.g: Righteous people who had died — death pictured as sleep.

n: After Jesus’s resurrection they come out of the tombs, enter Jerusalem, and appear to many. Christ is the firstfruits of the resurrection.
The Roman centurion and soldiers on guard, seeing the earthquake and all that happened, are terrified and confess: “Truly this was the Son of God.” Gentiles recognize what the leaders denied.

f.w: Truly this was the Son of God

n: Many women who had followed and supported Jesus from Galilee watch from a distance. They stay when the male disciples have fled.

f.g: Serving and supporting him, including financially.

n: Matthew names some of them: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, and the mother of James and John.

f.g: From Magdala on the Sea of Galilee; Jesus had cast seven devils out of her.

n: As evening approaches, Joseph of Arimathea, a wealthy secret disciple and council member, steps forward. Burial was needed before the Sabbath began at sunset.

f.g: A town in Judea, perhaps the Old Testament Ramah.

n: Joseph boldly asks Pilate for Jesus’s body, and Pilate grants it.

f.g: Crucified criminals were often left unburied; asking was a risky act of loyalty.

n: Joseph wraps the body in clean linen. John adds that Nicodemus brought spices.
He lays Jesus in his own new tomb cut into rock and rolls a large stone across the entrance.

f.g: Such tombs were cut into hillsides; the stone was often a large disc rolled in a channel.
sepulchre = tomb.

n: Mary Magdalene and the other Mary sit facing the tomb. They know exactly where Jesus was laid — important for the resurrection morning.

f.g: Opposite, facing.

n: The next day — the Sabbath — the chief priests and Pharisees go to Pilate.

f.g: Friday, the day to prepare for the Sabbath.

n: They remember Jesus said he would rise after three days. Ironically, his enemies remember his promise better than his disciples.

f.w: After three days I will rise again

f.g: Impostor.

n: They ask for the tomb to be secured so the disciples can’t steal the body and claim a resurrection.

f.g: Made secure.

f.w: the last error shall be worse than the first
f.g: This deception would be worse than his claim to be Messiah.

n: Pilate tells them to use their own guard and secure it as best they can.

f.g: Either “You have your own guard” (temple police) or “Take a guard” (Roman soldiers).

n: They seal the stone and post guards. Their precautions will only make the empty tomb more certain evidence.

f.g: A cord fixed with wax or clay seal across the stone, so tampering would show.
